title: The Frogs Returned in November
script: Narrator: [quietly] For years, the empty lot beside our neighbourhood flooded after heavy rain. Most residents called it a useless swamp and wanted it covered with concrete. Then a local ecology group invited us to visit just after sunset.

Narrator: We heard frogs before we saw them. The volunteers explained that the shallow water also slowed runoff, held insects eaten by birds, and supported plants adapted to wet soil. They did not claim the site was untouched nature; plastic waste and an invasive plant were obvious.

Narrator: [observant] The restoration began with questions. Where did the water enter? Which paths did residents use? Could rubbish be removed without damaging nests? A survey found that children crossed one unstable bank on their way to school, so safety became part of the plan.

Narrator: Over six weekends, volunteers removed waste, while trained staff managed the invasive plants. A raised walkway preserved access without draining the wet area. Native plants were added in stages, and survival rates were recorded rather than hidden.

Narrator: [reflective] Not every choice pleased everyone. Some residents still wanted more parking, and the first planting lost many seedlings during an unusually dry week. The team reported the loss and adjusted the watering plan.

Narrator: In November, the frogs returned in greater numbers, but the organisers avoided calling the project complete. One season could not prove long-term recovery. They scheduled monitoring for water quality, vegetation, and wildlife observations.
Narrator: [warmly] What changed most was the way we described the place. It was no longer “empty land” waiting for a profitable use. It was a working system with benefits, limits, and neighbours.
Narrator: The project taught us that care for nature needs more than affection. It needs evidence, patient maintenance, and decisions that include the people who live beside the habitat.
